source_refs.note: Book p. 223-224: 12.2.3 Limit at Infinity: (a) limit as x -> +inf (lim 1/x = 0), (b) limit as x -> -inf, Theorem lim a/x^p = 0 (p positive rational) with 'For example' (p. 224).

blocks.text: We have studied the limits of the functions \(f(x)\), \(f(x)g(x)\) and \(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\), when \(x \to c\) (a number). Let us see what happens to the limit of the function \(f(x)\) if \(c\) is \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\) (limits at infinity), i.e., when \(x \to +\infty\) and \(x \to -\infty\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
\(\infty\) (infinity) is not a number; we can never put \(x = \infty\). "\(x \to +\infty\)" means \(x\) takes larger and larger positive values (10, 100, 1000, ...) without any end. "\(x \to -\infty\)" means \(x\) takes negative values that grow larger and larger in size (\(-10, -100, -1000, \dots\)).
A limit at infinity asks: as \(x\) runs off in that direction, does \(f(x)\) settle down near one fixed number?

Let \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\), when \(x \ne 0\). This function has the property that the value of \(f(x)\) can be made as close as we please to zero when the number \(x\) is sufficiently large. We express this phenomenon by writing

blocks.text_alt: limit as x tends to infinity of 1 over x equals 0

blocks.caption: Our table (not in the book): as x grows, 1/x comes closer and closer to 0 but never equals 0.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read the table: each time \(x\) is multiplied by 10, \(\frac{1}{x}\) becomes ten times smaller. Whatever small distance from 0 you name, e.g. 0.000001, a large enough \(x\) (here \(x > 10^{6}\)) brings \(\frac{1}{x}\) closer to 0 than that. This is exactly what "as close as we please" means.
Note that \(\frac{1}{x}\) never becomes 0; the limit is the value it approaches, not a value it reaches.
This type of limits are handled in the same way as limits as \(x \to +\infty\), i.e.,

blocks.text_alt: limit as x tends to minus infinity of 1 over x equals 0, where x is not 0

blocks.caption: Our table (not in the book): for large negative x, 1/x is a small negative number that approaches 0.

blocks.text: The following theorem is useful for evaluating limits at infinity.
Theorem: Let \(p\) be a positive rational number. If \(x^{p}\) is defined, then

blocks.text_alt: limit as x tends to plus infinity of a over x to the power p equals 0
limit as x tends to minus infinity of a over x to the power p equals 0

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the theorem true? The numerator \(a\) stays fixed, while the size of the denominator \(x^{p}\) grows without bound (because \(p > 0\)). A fixed number divided by a larger and larger number gets closer and closer to 0.
Why "if \(x^{p}\) is defined"? For \(x \to -\infty\), some powers do not exist: e.g. \(x^{1/2} = \sqrt{x}\) is not a real number for negative \(x\), so \(\lim_{x\to -\infty}\frac{a}{\sqrt{x}}\) has no meaning. Odd roots such as \(\sqrt[5]{x}\) or \(\sqrt[3]{x}\) are defined for negative \(x\) too.
In the book's examples: \(a = 6\), \(p = 3\); and \(a = -5\), \(p = \frac{1}{5}\) (since \(\sqrt[5]{x} = x^{1/5}\)).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: This theorem is the reason behind the method of 12.2.5. Whenever you write \(\frac{10}{x} \to 0\) or \(\frac{50}{x^{3}} \to 0\), you are using it; you can write "\(\because \lim \frac{a}{x^{p}} = 0\)" as the reason.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\infty\) is not a number; \(x \to \pm\infty\) means \(x\) grows without bound in size, positive or negative.
2. \(\lim_{x\to \pm\infty}\frac{1}{x} = 0\).
3. Theorem: \(\lim_{x\to \pm\infty}\frac{a}{x^{p}} = 0\) for any real \(a\) and positive rational \(p\), whenever \(x^{p}\) is defined.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Substituting \(x = \infty\) as if it were a number, e.g. writing \(\frac{1}{\infty}\) as a final answer. Write the limit, 0.
2. Thinking that \(\frac{a}{x^{p}}\) tends to \(a\) or to \(\infty\). The numerator is fixed and the denominator grows, so the fraction tends to 0.
3. Using the theorem for \(x \to -\infty\) with an even root such as \(\sqrt{x}\), which is not defined for negative \(x\).
